data_status: STRICT MODE: this dataset contains only values that were compared with, or ingested directly from, retrieved sources: JPL (SSD, SBDB), NASA (NSSDC fact sheets and mission catalog, Small Spacecraft SoA report 2026, SLS page, Apollo 11 press kit, NTRS papers, ), ULA, ESA, NIST, and the Launch Library 2 aggregator. Records carry source_authority/confidence where the source is an aggregator or vendor-reported compilation. Recalled, estimated and fictional values (optimizer catalog, costs, engine/vehicle specs without a retrievable source, the user-supplied SpaceX table) are not included. Derived values are computed only from verified inputs and are labelled derived.

record.name: Rock Abrasion Tool (RAT)
record.description: The Rock Abrasion Tool (RAT) is a device containing a grinding wheel designed to remove dust and weathered material from the surface of a rock to expose a fresh surface. The fresh surface, which is more likely to represent the original rock before alteration, can then be studied by the other rover instruments. It is mounted on the rover arm, or instrument deployment device and is placed by the arm against the target rock. The RAT is 7 cm in diameter and 10 cm long. It uses two diamond matrix wheels. Each wheel has two teeth which cut out a circular area as the head rotates at high speed. The grinding wheels can also slowly revolve around each other, sweeping the two circular areas over a 4.5 cm diameter cutting region. The wheels can penetrate by fractions of a millimeter as commanded, creating a hole as deep as 0.5 cm. Penetration into the rock is slow and designed to minimize alteration of the petrologic fabric, chemistry, or mineralogy. Currents and temperatures will be monitored during the grinding opeation to infer information on the rock properties. Grinding operations take about 2 hours for a dense basalt.
